newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain basks under low inflation, EMU optimism.
newsitem.headline: Spain basks under low inflation, EMU optimism.

text.p: Enthusiasm electrified financial markets on Thursday as the country's greatest ambition -- to join Europe's single currency in 1999 -- appeared more within reach than ever before.

Stocks shot to a historic high and bond yields plunged to an all-time low after inflation, Spain's thorniest EMU challenge, turned in an unexpectedly tame October performance and added to evidence that the nation was well on track for monetary union.

Praise gushed from even that hardest-hearted of critics, the Bundesbank, after Spain's national statistics institute announced on Thursday that consumer prices had risen a modest 0.1 percent during October for a 3.5 percent year-on-year rise.
This was better than the 0.2 percent and 3.6 percent economists polled by Reuters had forecast.

The benign report ignited hopes that the inflation rate would sink beneath the government's target of 3.4 percent at the end of the year and that the Bank of Spain might sanction a further reduction in its 6.75 percent money market rate.
"The Bank of Spain has room to cut 25 basis points before the end of the year. Food prices have behaved better than predicted," said Xavier Segura, economist at Caixa de Catalunya.

The premium for 10-year Spanish government bonds over their German equivalents contracted to a new low of 145 basis points from 330 at the beginning of March, reflecting market views that the extra risk of holding Spanish debt was declining.
The IBEX index of 35 leading shares quickly followed suit, opening at a record high of 4,495.70.

Adding to the swell of positive sentiment, top economic officials suggested Spain was on its way to EMU, and even Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing was brimming with praise for Madrid's hard work.
"Spain has made a lot of effort which deserves the applause of everyone," he told reporters after addressing bankers in the northern Spanish town of Pamplona.
His praise for Spain contrasted starkly with his criticism of France and his warning that Germany itself must try harder.

Spain's six-month-old conservative government has pledged to ensure the nation joins the single currency at launch and has backed this up with an austere budget for 1997, containing both spending cuts and liberalisation measures.

Many economists have had faith Spain would manage to pass the Maastricht tests on long-term interest rates, foreign exchange stability, deficit and debt-to-gross domestic product ratios, but they worried it might stumble on inflation.

Budget Office chief Jose Barea said after Thursday's inflation figures that Spain would meet the criteria on inflation, deficit and long-term interest rates, and that debt would not determine the selection of entrants in the Economic and Monetary Union.
"We are in shape to reach the deficit objective in 1997. We will also fulfil the criteria on inflation and on rates," Barea said at the Pamplona seminar.
And Economy Secretary Cristobal Montoro added that inflation would likely end 1996 even below the government's target.
"The fall in October helps to confirm the achievement of the government's target. It's almost certain now that the CPI will end December below 3.4 percent," he told reporters.
